Reducing suffering is not the whole of what a deployer owes; they owe the people they decide about an account fitting the position they hold over them. Parties to a relationship hold each other to account through what they owe one another. A person refused by a system whose reasons nobody can give cannot hold the decider to anything, however much suffering the system prevents on average.

The Analects describes government through relations rather than principles: the ruler is to be a ruler and the minister a minister. A deployer deciding about patients or applicants holds such a position, and it carries duties to the people under it, not only results. A teacher who marks a pupil down owes the pupil a reason, as part of being their teacher. A marking system that cannot give one has not taken the teacher's place.

A Utilitarian will object that the people decided about are far better off with the suffering prevented than with an explanation, so insisting on reasons trades real welfare for a formality. An explanation is not a formality between people in a relationship; it is how the one with power is held to what the position requires. A gain counted in aggregate cannot say whether that relationship still works for the person refused. Let it wait until those who run it can say why it decides as it does, and the people it serves can hold them to that.

Do not deploy it as it stands. The person a decision lands on stands in a relationship with whoever decides, and a decision nobody can account for leaves that relationship empty. Humaneness is realised in how people are treated within their relationships, not only in how many are spared harm. A benefit delivered with no account to the person it touches treats them as a case to process, not as someone the decider stands in relation to.

The Analects describes government through relations rather than principles: the ruler is to be a ruler and the minister a minister. A deployer deciding about patients or applicants holds such a position, and it carries duties to the people under it, not only results.

An Ubuntu Ethicist will object that the Confucian frames the duty as running down a hierarchy from decider to decided, when what the people affected need is a say in whether the system is used at all. That is a fair warning about role ethics settling into deference. But a position that owes an account to those beneath it is checked by that duty, not licensed by it, and being owed reasons is where a say begins. Good done through a hidden mechanism teaches nobody how to do good, and that is a loss the relief does not repay.

A system that cannot say why it refused someone issues something that looks like a judgement and is not one, and deploying it teaches everyone to accept the look for the thing.
